1.1: 1.1 Argument. He writes a friendly letter to Philemon on behalf of Onesimus his servant, writing to him from the city of Rome, from prison, by the aforesaid Onesimus. Paul, a prisoner. He does not say 'Apostle,' which is the name of dignity, but prisoner, which is the name of humility: because he does not command but begs. For here there is intercession for Onesimus: therefore he mentions the things of humility, beginning from his own injury, so as to give dignity to his Epistle. For as to be bound for the cause of sin is a reproach, so on the contrary to endure the chains of custody for Christ is the greatest glory. At that time, therefore, he was in custody. Therefore he calls himself a prisoner.
1.5: 1.5 Which you have. Because he believed in Christ and loved him; believed in the saints and loved them, and so through works of faith and charity served Christ and the saints.
1.6: 1.6 That the communication. As if to say: You have faith and charity in Christ and in the saints, so that the communication of your faith becomes evident, that is, that your faith shares with our faith; or, that what you communicate to others from your faith may be evident. And this, In the acknowledgment of every. That is, may it be so evident, that by this it may be recognized that every good is in you through Christ, that is, the sufficiency of all goods. So that: I am mindful of you, and give thanks in my prayers concerning this, that the communication of your faith, that is, the working of the faith by which you serve Christ and the saints, may become evident in the acknowledgment which is. In Christ Jesus. That is, with knowledge of the eternal good, so that it is awaited as reward. For the Apostle prays this, that his working be done with knowledge of goodness, that is, that he work with such a mind as to look forward in the future for Jesus Christ as reward from it, not temporal recompense.
1.7: 1.7 The bowels of the saints. That is, the dearest sons of the saints, or, the affection of the saints toward you, inclined, has rested in you, namely, consoling, and has been refreshed, because they have found you good in all things.
1.10: 1.10 I beseech you. It is a great thing if one not of low but of high station stoops and beseeches. An old man. To an old man, by likeness of age, one ought rather to yield.
1.11: 1.11 Who once, etc. CHRYSOSTOM. See how prudently he confesses the offense of Onesimus himself, so that by this very thing he may extinguish the anger of the master; he does not say: 'Now he will be useful to you,' lest the other not believe, but he also introduced his own person, so that from this Philemon might more worthily hope for better things. For if he will be useful to Paul, who requires so great a diligence of virtue and perfection, how much more to his master.
1.12: 1.12 That my own bowels, etc. The Apostle, being in custody, baptized Onesimus the fugitive, who ran back to divine help, seeing in him a hope of usefulness: whom he so commends as to signify that his own heart is received in him.
1.15: 1.15 Perhaps. He says 'perhaps' because human things are doubtful, and there could have been another reason why God so disposed.
1.16: 1.16 Especially to me. To me, your teacher: Onesimus the brother, having offended his own master, fled to the Apostle to the end that, his sins blotted out, he might return useful, so much so that he might become not only equal to his master in merits but a brother to the teacher himself. And lest Philemon (because he is the master) be puffed up against the servant, he humbles him, saying: A brother both in the flesh, because all are from one Adam, and in the Lord through faith.
1.18: 1.18 Put that to my account. Now he removes every excuse, when he says that it should be charged to him if he has either harmed or owes anything. So, brother, may I have joy of you in the Lord. That is, I will rejoice in you in the kingdom of God, if you do what I ask. And what that is, he adds: Refresh my bowels, etc. Confident in your obedience. He challenges him by such flattery that he does no more than is asked of him. For it usually happens that one who sees that good is thought of him shows himself better.
1.22: 1.22 At the same time. To make him more careful and more ready to obey, he signifies that he will come to him: because even this can move him to pardon. For the absent are usually despised.
